items.title: Can agents write inference engines from scratch in 12 hours and beat vLLM?
items.story_key: model:vllm|title:can agents write inference engines from scratch in 12 hours and beat vllm
items.content_excerpt: Ultra-long-horizon agentic coding benchmark that build inference stacks from scratch Steven Gao 1 , Rulin Shao 1 , Keisuke Kamahori 1 , Yuetai Li 1 , Yufei Gao 1 , Atindra Jha 2 , Junjie Oscar Yin 1 , Shihang Li 1 , Radha Poovendran 1 , Jure Leskovec 2 , Hannaneh Hajishirzi 1 , Pang Wei Koh 1 , Luke Zettlemoyer 1 , Stephanie Wang 1 , Baris Kasikci 1 Would you bet that a coding agent could write an inference engine from scratch in 12 hours and beat vLLM? The best agents already can. Opus 5's servers passed verification and beat the production baseline in 71% of its runs, with speedups of up to 25.9× on speech recognition and 4.9× on omni chat. The next best model did so in 24% of runs, and no model produced a correct server on every attempt. Humanity's Last System (HLS) is the ultra-long-horizon agentic coding benchmark behind those numbers. Each task gives an agent a live GPU sandbox, with up to 8 H200s and up to 36 hours, and asks it to build a serving system specialized to one model, one hardware platform and one production workload. HLS then deploys the agent's final commit in a fresh container, runs the task's timed workload against it, checks the outputs against a trusted reference, and scores its speed against a baseline. A server that fails the check scores zero. The introduction describes the tasks, the verifiers and our results, and hlsbench.com has the leaderboard and over 150 agent trajectories. HLS reads two files: hls.toml in the checkout, which says where jobs run and which agent builds, and a secrets file that holds your keys. The secrets file names each key once. The [grants] table gives the Hugging Face token to the step that downloads model weights: This runs one full round of the benchmark on the sample task, which serves a 0.5B model and gives the agent at most an hour. HLS downloads the model and data, builds the container images, starts the agent in its sandbox, then packages, serves, verifies and scores what the agent committed. The sample task asks for an H200; on other GPUs, name yours after the task, for example --task.hardware.accelerator.kind=L40S . If you stop the command, the run keeps going. uv run hls status runs/sample_task/<id> shows where it is, and uv run hls resume runs/sample_task/<id> follows it again. uv run hls view serves a web page of every run in the store. The seven benchmark tasks run the same way; docs/tasks.md lists them. Before the first run of multitenant_slo, tab_completion, multimodal_tts or agentic_codin

items.title: Compiling web applications into verified operations for AI agents
items.story_key: story|title:compiling web applications into verified operations for ai agents
items.content_excerpt: A web agent pays a language model to read the page at every step: first to work out what it can do there, then to find out whether its last action worked. Solid-state web execution removes both. On arrival at a page it has never seen, the Protocolis compiler turns the page's controls into typed operations; the model picks one; the compiler runs it, reads the page again and reports what actually changed. Compilation uses no model inference, no site-specific code and no prior visit. To our knowledge it is the first such compiler in operation. We tested it against the browser tools and agents in common use, as shipped, across three model sizes and three task lengths, with its memory and learning switched off. On long tasks that every system attempted, its default mode completed 76 percent (80 of 105); the best alternative in each comparison completed 46 percent. It was the most stable system tested: it never fell below 55 percent in any condition, while every alternative fell to 28 percent or lower. The cheapest alternative on the same model cost 1.9 to 26 times as much per completed task. On a small model it cost less than every alternative on a frontier model, in 30 of 30 pairings, and matched or exceeded its completion rate in 24. When it reported a long task finished, the judge disagreed less than half as often as with the alternatives (22 against 56 percent). Every result is a first visit, the least favourable setting for the design. We publish the tasks, the judging rules and the outcome of all 3,443 counted runs. Patent-pending, in production with paying customers, offered for acquisition. Evaluation access on request: get in touch .

items.title: Announcing vLLM-GR: Efficient Inference for Generative Recommendation
items.summary: vLLM-GR extends vLLM to serve generative recommendation models with accelerator-side beam search, catalog constraints, and shared KV caching across candidate paths.
items.story_key: model:vllm|title:announcing vllm gr efficient inference for generative recommendation
items.content_excerpt: Today we’re introducing vLLM-GR , an open-source inference and serving framework built on vLLM for generative recommendation models. Consider a video feed. Given a viewer’s history, a model such as OneRec can generate a semantic ID (SID) for a video the viewer might watch next. To assemble a feed, the application needs a set of candidates. vLLM-GR extends vLLM’s model execution and paged key-value (KV) cache with beam search that explores multiple candidate IDs in one request. The overview shows how recommendation models generate item IDs or score supplied candidates. The OneRec-1.7B example below follows the generation path, from a viewer’s history to 128 candidate SIDs. A recommendation service has to turn a long interaction history into a set of candidates within a single request’s latency budget. Generating each item ID may take only a few tokens, yet the engine must explore many paths and return items the application can serve. vLLM-GR builds its recommendation search into the vLLM engine. vLLM supplies the scheduler, model execution, and paged KV cache. vLLM-GR adds a beam session that spans the whole search and keeps track of how candidate paths branch. EngineCore owns each beam session from admission to completion. The scheduler dispatches prefill and decode stages to a worker. At each stage, the model runner scores the next token and beam selection records the score and parent of each surviving path. The next decode uses those parent indices to read the right KV state. One request returns two candidates with beam widths of 2 → 3 → 2. The catalog filters out A1 · B1 because no item starts with that prefix. A full-vocabulary search skips this filter. The SIDs and scores are illustrative. In the prefill–decode–decode (PDD) pipeline, the scheduler admits a BeamSearch() request and dispatches its prefill stage to the worker. Prefill scores the first SID component while the host prepares decode 1. During decode 1, the host prepares decode 2. The second decode inherits the selected parents’ suffix KV and completes two SIDs. Green marks the component selected at each stage. The benchmarks measure P99 latency to show how beam width and batch size affect tail latency for generative recommendation. The two overview charts hold the input length at 1,024 tokens and compare beam widths of 256 and 128 at batch sizes 1, 4, and 8 across four NVIDIA GPUs and two Ascend NPUs. items.title: Built for trust and control: Powering the next wave of AI agents across Google Workspace and Google Cloud
items.summary:
For over 20 years, we have protected 4 billion users and 13 million organizations in Workspace, and critical enterprise and government systems on Google Cloud. From personal and financial records to board materials, regulated workloads, applications, and AI models, those safeguards protect what matters most. Blocking >99.9% of spam, phishing, and malware, alongside encryption and data residency, follows one principle: your data is yours, and you should always know and decide who can access it.

That trust has powered one of the world’s largest developer ecosystems. Workspace APIs now handle more than 2.8 trillion calls a month, and public Google Drive API traffic alone is more than two-and-a-half times the volume of 2022. More than 18 billion reads from Drive each day come from API callers. Traditional REST APIs were built for human-paced apps where a valid OAuth token implied user intent. As AI agents shift from reading information to acting autonomously at machine speed across email, documents, datasets, and cloud infrastructure, a valid token is no longer enough. Policy checks, data boundaries, and human confirmation have to live in the request path. 

Today, Workspace MCP servers and the Workspace CLI are generally available alongside Google Cloud Agent Gateway and unified protections across Workspace and Google Cloud. Builders get modern, agent-ready interfaces, and organizations get the visibility and control to adopt AI agents with confidence.

Purpose-built interfaces: Workspace MCP servers, Workspace CLI, and Cloud Agent Gateway

To help developers build reliable agents faster without forcing security teams to compromise, we are bringing agent-native interfaces to Workspace and Google Cloud:

  • Workspace MCP servers: Now generally available, dedicated remote servers for Gmail, Google Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Chat, and Tasks. Builders get one standard interface with built-in permission and DLP checks, and native human-in-the-loop (HITL) confirmations for sensitive actions. They also reject non-agent OAuth clients and work with Model Armor, Google Cloud’s prompt-injection screening service.

  • Workspace CLI: Now generally available for local agents, terminal workflows, and automation, providing structured JSON outputs and scoped OAuth sign-in across Workspace services.

  • Google Cloud Agent Gateway: A protocol-native gateway for LLM, MCP, and Agent2Agent (A2A) traffic on Google Cloud. It verifies Agent Identities against Agent Registry, enforces IAM policies and default-deny outbound rules, and screens requests with Model Armor.

Together, these interfaces give AI agents open, protocol-native paths built on standards like MCP and A2A. Permissions, confirmations, prompt screening, and audit logging happen automatically, while traditional apps continue to run on existing REST APIs.

Consistent controls across every agent workflow

Those interfaces sit on a unified security model across Workspace and Google Cloud, with core controls shipping today:

  1. Policy checks on every request: Under our new Workspace AI Tools Addendum, AI agents must use Workspace MCP servers or the Workspace CLI rather than existing REST APIs. Technical enforcement begins on February 1, 2027, giving builders time to transition. Every call is checked against your organization’s Workspace permissions, DLP rules, and classification labels. On Google Cloud, Agent Gateway enforces IAM and default-deny outbound rules at the protocol layer and routes custom checks through Service Extensions to Identity-Aware Proxy, your own policy engine, or third-party security tools.

  2. Separate agent identities and limits: Admins and users need to tell an AI agent apart from a traditional app or a person, and cap what it can do. Agents connecting to Workspace must use dedicated OAuth client IDs, paired with least-privilege scopes, time-limited approvals (coming soon), and usage quotas (billing begins on April 1, 2027). On Google Cloud, agents receive their own Agent Identity in Agent Registry with no shared or long-lived keys, bounded by IAM policies and organization, folder, and project quotas. Those identities can also carry user-delegated authorization into Workspace when accessing mail or files.

  3. People stay in charge of high-impact actions: Routine work like creating drafts or summarizing documents runs autonomously, while critical changes require a person to sign off. In Workspace, MCP servers and the CLI enforce explicit user confirmation before agents send email, change Drive sharing permissions, or make bulk edits. On Google Cloud, policy can require multi-factor authentication or human approval before reading sensitive Cloud Storage buckets, changing IAM permissions, or modifying production infrastructure.

  4. Clear visibility and revocation: A one-time consent screen is not enough when agents run continuously. Workspace administrators can view, audit, and revoke AI agents in the admin console, and users will soon be able to view agent activity and revoke access to their emails and files. On Google Cloud, Security Command Center, Agent Observability, Cloud Audit Logs, and Wiz surface unusual behavior. Revoking a Cloud Agent Identity or OAuth grant stops access immediately.

  5. Boundaries for your most sensitive data: Coming soon in Workspace, AI access restrictions extend Workspace DLP and client-side encryption protections to agents. This will allow admins and users to block agents from accessing messages in Gmail and specific files and folders in Drive. On Google Cloud, VPC Service Controls, Principal Access Boundaries, and Context-Aware Access keep sensitive data inside designated perimeters and verified devices.

  6. Strict rules on your data afterward: Our new Workspace AI Tools Addendum sets clear boundaries for AI tools using Workspace APIs. It does not allow permanent raw storage, model training, extended retention of derived data, or API scraping. Derived and user data are removed within a defined window and when a user disconnects. On Google Cloud, Sensitive Data Protection masks sensitive fields before data leaves, and customer-managed or external encryption keys let you cut off access to Cloud agent memory stores immediately.

Getting started

  • Workspace developers: Start building with the Workspace MCP and CLI configuration guide, implement user confirmations via MCP and prompt-injection protection such as Model Armor, and review the Workspace AI Tools Addendum.

  • Workspace administrators: Review connected apps and agents, configure DLP policies for your users, and monitor OAuth activity logs in the admin console.

  • Google Cloud customers: Register Agent Identities in Agent Registry, place Agent Gateway and Model Armor in front of agents and MCP servers, configure MFA or human approval for sensitive actions, and review IAM, VPC Service Controls, and quota limits.

With Workspace MCP servers and the Workspace CLI generally available alongside Google Cloud’s agent protections, developers have an open, modern platform to build on. Organizations get the visibility and control to scale AI agents with confidence.

items.title: Antiphony: A Dual-Process Agent for Deepfake Video Detection with Real-Video Calibration
items.summary: Reliable video deepfake detection requires generalization to unseen generators while limiting false alarms on authentic footage. Although existing detectors capture diverse visual cues, they may produce overconfident errors under generator shift, limiting the reliability of confidence-based fusion. Threshold calibration is further complicated by shifts in authentic capture domains and the lack of future-generator examples. To address these challenges, we present Antiphony, a framework that combines calibrated fusion of four visual experts with selective investigation. Authentic videos serve as a shared reference for score fusion and threshold calibration, enabling threshold updates without target deepfakes. For this expert-fusion stage, we establish finite-sample false-alarm control when the scoring procedure is fixed independently of calibration and authentic samples are exchangeable. To refine decisions near the calibrated threshold, a tool-using multimodal investigator examines these videos and contributes an additional fusion score. We train the investigator on generator-held-out predictions and counterfactual expert outputs, to improve robustness to unreliable expert evidence. Across six benchmark protocols, Antiphony achieves a mean benchmark score of 88.3%, exceeding the strongest evaluated MLLM and conventional detector baselines by 14.7 and 11.5 points, respectively. It also outperforms ARGUS by 20.2 points on average and by 3.6 balanced-accuracy points on FaceVid's 20 unseen generators.

items.title: Rethinking the Evaluation of Contrastive Decoding for Hallucination Mitigation in Multimodal Large Language Models
items.summary: Contrastive decoding (CD) mitigates object hallucination in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by contrasting token distributions under different conditions to adjust token scores. However, existing generative and discriminative benchmarks primarily measure final task scores, which can be confounded by candidate filtering, changes in generation trajectories, and response biases, making it difficult to isolate the effects of the underlying contrastive adjustments. To address these limitations while complementing existing evaluations, we introduce CONCOR (Contrastive Correction Evaluation), a controlled benchmark that directly evaluates the competition between ground-truth and different types of hallucinated candidates using the Contrastive Grounding Margin (CGM). CGM also enables analysis of directional consistency, composition, and reliability of contrastive corrections. Our evaluation reveals that existing CD methods exhibit distinct correction behaviors: some consistently favor ground-truth candidates, whereas others produce strong corrections but also introduce more errors. Crucially, these differences help explain their contrasting responses to increased contrast strength, which improves some methods while degrading others. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating the contrastive correction itself, rather than relying solely on final-output performance, and CONCOR provides a controlled and interpretable framework for understanding and improving CD methods for hallucination mitigation.

items.title: FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment
items.summary: Model alignment is the primary safety and security mechanism for enforcing refusal of malicious prompts in modern foundation models; yet, existing adversarial evaluations implicitly assume underlying hardware integrity. In this paper, we present FATCAT, the first physical fault-injection attacks capable of eliminating refusal in modern large language and vision-language models. Specifically, we present a non-invasive electromagnetic (EM) fault injection attack targeting GPU-accelerated Systems-on-Chip with physical access, requiring neither software execution privileges nor model-layer access. By leveraging an autonomous Radio Frequency (RF) side-channel trigger to synchronize EM faults to the prompt prefill phase, the attack corrupts safety-critical memory transactions across off-chip LPDDR5 DRAM and on-chip LPDDR physical interfaces without crashing the system while preserving model coherence. Evaluated on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and AGX Thor running Llama 3.2 1B and Gemma 3 1B, localized physical faults reliably force models to fulfill restricted requests, demonstrating that model-level alignment provides no robust security guarantees without hardware-level fault tolerance. Finally, we demonstrate the physical-world consequences of this vulnerability on an active 6-DoF robotic manipulator controlled by a SmolVLA vision-language-action policy. Our attack silently corrupts the model forcing the arm into abrupt, hazardous lunges; in two instances the robotic arm attempted to pinch the paper author -- proving that hardware faults can directly translate into real physical harm.

items.story_key: story|title:data modeling best practices for an agentic cdp part 1 the data foundation
items.content_excerpt: A customer saved a jacket to their wishlist on your site 9 days ago. This morning its price dropped 30%. Should you let them know? That depends on your goal. If you want first-time buyers to come back for a second purchase, the alert could help. If you're growing lifetime value and this customer usually pays full price, the discount may cost more than it earns. Whatever the goal, an agent needs six answers about this one person before it makes the call (Figure 1). Figure 1. The goal frames one price-drop decision, and the decision needs answers from six kinds of data. If you're getting customer data ready for an Agentic CDP, start here. At Databricks, we work with many brands on this, and the data model is usually the hardest part. This post is for the data architect who designs the stack that marketers, and now agents, build on. This is Part 1 of a two-part series. Part 1: the modeling steps, from raw data to omnichannel activation. Part 2: mapping B2C and B2B datasets, attributes and use cases onto the model. An Agentic CDP needs everything a traditional CDP needs: the right sources, clean data, one identity per customer and golden profiles marketers trust. If you've built a CDP before, that work carries over. If you haven't, it's the place to start. What changes is who does the work and how fast the data has to be right. Agents take on more of the work, such as matching records and drafting audiences, while people choose the sources, review the matches and approve what goes out. And because an agent decides for one person in seconds, a gap in the data turns into a bad decision just as fast. Databricks built CustomerLake around the same idea. Data teams can define trusted datasets and models once through Databricks and Unity Catalog. Marketers can then use purpose-built interfaces to ask questions, build segments, and activate audiences faster without working around IT or exporting data into unmanaged tools. Here's the flow we recommend. It's a medallion architecture with one important rule: identity resolution runs after silver, and the canonical ID it creates becomes the join key for gold. You build the layers with Spark Declarative Pipelines , keep them on schedule with Lakeflow Jobs and govern every layer in Unity Catalog . Figure 2. One governed path from raw data to connected channels, keyed by one canonical ID. Brands have asked for years why they can't own their identity graph and run deterministic matching on their own data. items.title: Skip the DRAM Tier: MoRI UMBP Runs the Agentic KV Cache on NVMe
items.summary: On AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs, a MoRI UMBP KV pool on NVMe matched a DRAM pool of the same size within 1% for Kimi-K3 on vLLM, and drives that hold a day of agent KV cost less than DRAM that holds 31 minutes.
items.story_key: story|title:skip the dram tier mori umbp runs the agentic kv cache on nvme
items.content_excerpt: Most of the traffic in agentic serving is multi-turn sessions that resend long prefixes. In the AgentX benchmark replaying real Claude Code sessions, the median turn is 142K input tokens, and over 96% of those tokens are a prefix the server has already seen [3] . A KV cache hit means the prefill node only has to process the small delta. A miss forces a full recomputation of the prefix, which burns GPU time and delays the first token. In our 42 runs of Kimi-K3 on vLLM, raising the KV cache hit rate by 1% of prompt tokens, for example from 95% to 96%, was worth about 10% more throughput (Figure 3). A KV cache hit needs the session’s prefix to still be in memory when its next turn arrives. With dozens of sessions open at once, memory runs out. GPU memory goes first, and host DRAM is the usual next tier. But DRAM fills too: Kimi-K3 wrote 2.3 to 4.6 TB of KV to the pool an hour in our runs, so a 1.8 TB DRAM pool, which lists at about $76,000, holds only the last 23 to 47 minutes of it. That led us to a simple question: why not skip the DRAM tier and put vLLM’s KV pool straight on NVMe? We tried it on AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs with UMBP, the KV cache pool in AMD’s open-source MoRI library. At the same size, NVMe matched DRAM’s throughput within 1% on Kimi-K3, in two sets of runs on different machines (Figure 1). On a second workload with longer prompts, NVMe came within 1% of a DRAM pool of the same size. The NVMe pool has no DRAM tier: DRAM only buffers new KV on its way to the drives and stages reads, about 80 GB against the DRAM pool’s 1.8 TB. And NVMe’s cost follows the KV it writes, not the KV it holds, so drives rated for Kimi-K3’s writes cost less than that DRAM pool and hold a full day of KV. “Agentic workloads keep sessions open for minutes or hours, and their KV cache quickly outgrows GPU memory and host DRAM. Results like these, with NVMe keeping up with DRAM at the same pool size, change how we think about sizing KV cache capacity in AI clusters. We’re glad to see this work done in the open, in vLLM and MoRI.” — Dennis Kennetz, Principal Infrastructure Engineer, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure DeepSeek already keeps agent KV caches on SSD: the deployment notes for its DeepInfer engine describe three days of retention for agent traffic, on about 14.4 TB of SSD per GPU [4] . This work references DeepInfer for the idea of keeping the KV cache on SSD and for two of its techniques, layer-wise loading and bounded replay, which we test on vLLM below. Figure 1.

items.title: Habitats: A Framework for Open-Ended Evolution of Agent Objectives
items.summary: Designing what an agent should optimize can be as difficult as optimizing the agent itself. Existing language-model-based reward-generation methods typically refine objectives for predefined tasks and couple the decision of what to explore with the synthesis of how to implement it, potentially narrowing the resulting behavioral repertoire. We introduce Habitats, a framework for open-ended evolution of executable agent objectives. Habitats maintains a population of reward-policy pairs and evaluates every policy under every population reward, producing a cross-fitness matrix that exposes self-mastery, transfer, and functional diversity. A population-level Planner uses this information to select parent rewards and issue targeted mutation directives, while a separate Mutator translates those directives into validated reward programs. We evaluate Habitats in a discrete Card Sandbox and three continuous-control environments (Cart-Pole, Hopper, and Cheetah) against Independent Generation and Direct Mutation baselines. Across four environments and three random seeds, Habitats achieves the highest macro-averaged final Specialist Quality and Behavioral Diversity, with final diversity reaching 1.8x that of Direct Mutation and 2.5x that of Independent Generation. Finally, across ten downstream objectives unseen during evolution, frozen Habitats policy libraries achieve higher paired win rates than size-matched Direct Mutation and Independent Generation libraries at 10,000 adaptation episodes, while also surpassing task-specific policies trained from scratch for 20,000 episodes. These results suggest that separating population-level planning from reward synthesis enables the discovery of diverse, learnable, and reusable behaviors.

items.title: Precision-Aware Learning Rate Transfer Across Block Count in LLM Post-Training
items.summary: The post-training of pretrained large language models, including supervised finetuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), and reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR), is very sensitive to the learning rate, and tuning it through grid search is costly in both computation and memory. In this work, we propose \textbf{TipSweep}, a method to transfer the learning rate across the number of trainable transformer blocks. To do so efficiently, we search for the best learning rate by training only the last $k_0$ blocks (in our experiments, typically $k_0=1$), and provide scaling rules that predict the optimal learning rate when training any set of $k$ blocks, including when $k=L$ (the full transformer). Across experiments with models ranging from 1 to 7 billion parameters, we observe that the optimal learning rate follows precision-dependent scaling rules: the optimal rate scales approximately as $k^{-1}$ with float32 (FP32) master weights, but as $k^{-1/2}$ when updates are applied directly to bfloat16 (BF16) weights without a master copy. We explain both rules using an analytical model that accounts for update rounding, under assumptions supported by profiling experiments. Finally, we develop two prototypes of the learning rate search for a 6.7-billion-parameter model. The first fits the search on a single consumer GPU with 16 GiB of memory. The second speeds up the search on a high-end GPU by evaluating all candidate learning rates in a single pass over the data, so that a five-candidate search takes about half the GPU hours of one full-depth ($k=L$) run.

items.title: How to build a knowledge factory for AI agents
items.summary: The knowledge factory is how LangChain keeps its agents' company knowledge current: agents flag what's missing, and a curator agent fixes it in the background.
items.story_key: story|title:how to build a knowledge factory for ai agents
items.content_excerpt: In order to make AI work for your company, the missing bit is not better models, it’s not just more context - it’s better knowledge. It’s knowledge of how your company works, what standards for operating you have in place, where data is stored and how it’s accessed. Your most efficient employees have this knowledge in their head. They know who to talk to, where to go to answer questions, why you do things in a particular way. That knowledge is often tacit, implicit, scattered - sometimes present only in their head, sometimes scattered across a variety of documents. In order to make AI work for your company, you need to collect, curate, and maintain a representation of that knowledge to pass to agents. The system that helps you do that is what we’re calling a knowledge factory. We’ve built this at LangChain in a few ways. Our internal GTM and content studio agents are powered by a knowledge factory. LangSmith Engine (our agent that runs over traces and suggests fixes) maintains a knowledge factory per agent as well. This blog shares our learnings. Knowledge is the reusable understanding we maintain so it can do that task correctly: what a metric means, which source to trust, or how we handle a particular situation. Sometimes written down, often not. A knowledge factory turns scattered documents and experience into knowledge that can become context for future work. So knowledge is a form of context that the agent will get, but it’s often not (and shouldn’t be) the only context the agent gets. Other types of context you already ingest/store reliably, and that can just be provided directly to the agent (see the section on quickly changing data below). The idea of software factories has risen sharply over the past year and a half. The idea is that rather than having your best engineers actually build software, they should build the factory (the systems) to help everyone at the company build software more efficiently. The actual building of the software can be done by agents. General knowledge work is now following a similar path. Agents are good enough to make presentations, launch videos, do outbound. You should be leveraging them as much as possible for those tasks. But in order for them to accomplish those tasks they need all that tacit, implicit, scattered knowledge. items.content_excerpt: Explore a new Project Genie experience for Google AI Ultra subscribers, featuring Genie 4, the Project Genie agent, and a community gallery. We are rolling out Genie 4 to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, offering more responsive, social, and interactive world generation. You can now use natural language to edit environments in real time, add native audio, and share your creations in our new community gallery. Visit the Project Genie website to start building your own worlds or join the waitlist if you are a Google AI Pro member. Earlier this year we introduced Project Genie , an experimental research prototype that lets you generate and explore interactive worlds. Early testers told us they wanted deeper control over what happens inside those worlds, and easier ways to build and share them. So today, we are rolling out a new Project Genie experience to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, making these worlds far more responsive, creative, and social. This update unlocks first-time access to Genie 4, new upgrades to Genie 3, the Project Genie agent which helps users build their vision, and a community gallery to discover, explore, and remix worlds. Project Genie brings together our most advanced world models alongside our Gemini models, empowering you to generate, step inside, and shape worlds directly from your browser. With Genie 4 , our most realistic and interactive world model yet, you can now prompt mid-session to change the world you created. Just type a new prompt while you navigate your world and you can edit your environments in real time. Shift the weather, drop in a character, or redirect the action. For the first time, Genie 4 pairs these visuals with real-time native audio that adapts as the scene unfolds, from ambient soundscapes to character dialogue. While Genie 4 delivers our highest-fidelity visuals, physics, and native audio, Genie 3 remains available in Project Genie’s model picker when you want longer runs or panorama-seeded spaces. Today’s Genie 3 updates include: Genie 3 uses real-time promptable events to connect different worlds into one continuous flight across forests, underwater ruins, and icy seas. See how 360-degree panorama grounding in Genie 3 keeps Petra’s canyon and facade consistent as you look around. Watch how Genie 3 combines longer runs, 360-degree panorama grounding, and real-time promptable events - transforming the world as you fly and even summoning a dragon to ride on command. items.title: claude-code v2.1.327
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added a confirmation before /install-github-app changes a repository
  • Added claude mcp add-json <name> - to read the server's JSON from stdin, so tokens can stay off the command line; not available inside a Claude Code session
  • Added a line when a resumed session's earlier messages can't be loaded
  • Added a list in /status of broken agent, skill, command and output style files, keybinding errors, an unavailable sandbox, ignored permission settings and hook matchers that never match
  • Added a note in /config when other settings override a row
  • Added x-claude-code-managed-settings-checksum to the gateway hint headers; sent where managed settings set CLAUDE_CODE_GATEWAY_HINT_HEADERS=1, including where they already do
  • Added support for naming a session's billing group with the attributionProject setting, for Claude apps gateways that set admin.billing_group_tag
  • Added /tui classic as the name for the non-fullscreen renderer; /tui default still works
  • Remote Control: Fixed stopping the server in worktree mode deleting a running session's git-ignored files, such as .env
  • Fixed self-hosted runners with --use-anthropic-git-proxy deleting a non-empty directory named by GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL at startup: the runner now keeps it, ignores the variable and warns
  • Fixed claude mcp add and claude mcp remove with project scope deleting other top-level keys from .mcp.json, such as $schema or another tool's servers
  • Fixed /export overwriting an existing file without asking: the dialog now asks, and /export <name> keeps the file and says to run /export
  • Fixed a command you had allowed still running after you pressed Stop, when the approval arrived after a restart, in cloud and self-hosted runner sessions with no feature flags loaded
  • Fixed Enter closing /teleport's load error screen
  • Fixed a click followed by Enter in /plugin installing or disabling a plugin
  • Fixed a half-typed ! command running on an extra Enter after the usage limit menu
  • Fixed some --disallowedTools rules with parentheses in their content
  • Fixed auto mode ignoring some wildcard PowerShell allow rules that name a script with .\, such as PowerShell(.\scripts\build.ps1 *)
  • Fixed a running Code Mode script in auto mode getting permission prompts and denials once Claude started a second script that auto mode also allowed
  • Changed some pre-started background sessions to be discarded after an account change
  • Changed a workflow paused at a usage limit in the terminal to stay paused after a login, until the earlier login returns or you type a prompt
  • Fixed a nested claude with its own token being refused by forceLoginOrgUUID: commands that don't get the session's token no longer get its CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_SCOPES; set it on any that need it
  • Fixed headless sessions losing stored messages on resume when a message was sent again with the same UUID after the process was killed
  • Fixed cases where a session resumed after an empty reply or a killed command lost an answer, or brought back a rewound prompt, after another crash or a move to the background
  • Fixed a remote session forgetting messages sent after Stop was pressed during a restart, if Claude Code then crashed
  • Fixed tasks created after /clear being lost, and cleared tasks coming back, when a cloud or self-hosted runner session with no feature flags loaded resumed later
  • Fixed a compaction right after a reply cut at the output token limit losing that reply's tool call and its result
  • Fixed a settings change from /config and similar commands failing to save with no warning; a line under the prompt now says so
  • Fixed /rewind closing without a word when some files could not be restored
  • Fixed pasted images being dropped when the prompt starts with a file path such as /tmp/a.txt
  • Fixed agents passed with --agents being lost once plugins loaded or reloaded
  • Fixed a plugin's agent being dropped when resuming a session from the --resume picker
  • Fixed Claude Code refusing to start when https_proxy or HTTPS_PROXY is a bare host:port and neither its input nor its output is a terminal (the desktop app, an SDK, cron)
  • Fixed Claude Code on Linux sometimes returning to the shell while restarting itself at startup, such as after the first sign-in to a Claude apps gateway or when turning on Code Mode
  • Fixed claude -p hanging before its first request when the fetch of a model's settings stalled, such as at a proxy; it now goes on without them after 10 seconds
  • Fixed the screen staying blank or frozen after a brief out-of-memory error
  • Fixed a rare display fault that could freeze the screen or end the session
  • Fixed cloud sessions breaking when a program left thousands of connections open to the session's network proxy
  • Fixed a turn hanging when a mod's $.model.complete or $.model.classify call met a usage limit: the call now gets the API's error at once; mods should handle that error
  • Fixed stalls on a compaction reply with thousands of unclosed tags and on some very long WebFetch URLs; WebFetch now refuses a URL over 2,000 characters before any permission prompt
  • Fixed a message with thousands of @ mentions stalling before Claude replies; only the first 100 mentions are now looked up as files
  • Fixed the prompt freezing after rejecting a write to a very large file; a rejected write now shows a short preview
  • Fixed a crash when a burst of keys reached the search box in /plugin
  • Fixed a false crash report and exit code when a suspended session resumes, or at exit, where a Linux security policy blocks a process from signalling itself
  • Fixed remote MCP servers staying disconnected after a longer outage such as a VPN drop: most servers on other machines reached by hostname over https are now retried in the background for about a day
  • Fixed Edit refusing with "File has not been read yet" after a compaction on unchanged files outside the project that Claude had already read in full
  • Fixed Grep repeating or skipping results when paging with head_limit and offset; content and count results are now sorted by file path
  • Fixed Read failing on Jupyter notebooks that contain an output of an unknown type
  • Fixed NotebookEdit removing the notebook file's final newline
  • Fixed the Read tool reporting 512KB instead of the real size when a file of 10 MB or more is too large to read at once
  • Fixed the Bash tool's diff of changed files not naming files that are binary, too large or too many to show
  • Fixed artifact publishes failing with "the source file changed between approval and publish" when a synced or remote-backed folder had only changed the file's timestamp
  • Fixed a new artifact that you approved being refused in a cloud scheduled task's session, in organizations that require approval of each new artifact
  • Fixed a new artifact being refused after an app built on the Agent SDK approved it, in organizations that require approval of each new artifact
  • Fixed /artifacts showing part of your list, or "No artifacts yet", when a request for more of the list failed: it now tries again, then warns if it can't load the whole list
  • Fixed in-process agent teammates on a different model from the lead compacting at the lead's context limit and on the wrong model; they now use their own limit and model, at that model's rate
  • Fixed a finished subagent resuming on the model and effort of a sibling subagent that messaged it
  • Fixed the main conversation not being told a background agent had finished when the subagent that started it ended by itself without reading the result, outside auto mode
  • Fixed Claude reporting a background agent as still running when it had waited 30 seconds or more on a permission prompt in the desktop app, on the web and in the SDK
  • Fixed Claude not being told in auto mode when a background agent's reply to a follow-up message was dropped, and reduced repeat wake-ups there from agents waiting on background commands
  • Fixed the desktop app, Claude Code on the web and VS Code showing a raw task notification as a subagent's prompt after its background task woke it
  • Fixed messages sent from another session with "later" priority joining the running turn, instead of waiting for it to end, in Remote Control and Claude Desktop sessions
  • Fixed messages to cloud and Remote Control sessions being reported as failed with a stale address after a timeout or rate limit; Claude now says when a message may have arrived
  • Fixed cloud sessions giving no error when a UserPromptSubmit hook blocks a message sent while Claude works
  • Fixed failing hooks showing nothing: SubagentStop in background agents, SessionEnd at /clear and /resume, and CwdChanged and FileChanged in fullscreen
  • Fixed a Stop hook that failed to run being shown as having reported a problem
  • Fixed focus view keeping a finished reply hidden while a Stop hook was running
  • Fixed Claude getting a long managed PostToolUse hook output twice when a mod added context to the tool call
  • Fixed /model listing the wrong models in some terminal sessions when a project's .claude/settings.json sets ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to an LLM gateway
  • Fixed /statusline writing to ~/.claude/settings.json when CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR points to another folder
  • Fixed claudeMdExcludes patterns on Windows not matching a path whose drive letter is written in the other case
  • Fixed claude agents and claude rm refusing to remove a fully pushed session ("The worktree has unpushed commits") when its worktree has a file or folder named HEAD at the top level
  • Fixed long ListAgents results hiding most sessions on accounts with many cloud or Remote Control sessions: long lists now come in pages
  • Fixed slow turns in resumed sessions for organizations with tens of thousands of connector tool permissions
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed claude -p started by a session's script or hook waiting out rate limits, because it inherited the session's own retry setting
  • Fixed the spend limit menu reporting a changed limit when the server refused it
  • Fixed a second x on a task's details in /tasks stopping the next task too
  • Fixed Esc being ignored on a permission prompt that had just appeared
  • Fixed lists that load their rows late sometimes ignoring Enter and the arrow keys
  • Fixed /autofix-pr holding the keyboard after Esc while it stopped the cloud session; the dialog now closes at once, and a stop that fails is reported afterwards with a link
  • Fixed a blank screen and stray mouse codes in the shell after quitting with ctrl+c just after ← opens the agents view
  • Fixed Ctrl+C right after the trust question leaving the terminal in fullscreen
  • Fixed the shell flashing on screen when ← opens the agents view in fullscreen mode
  • Fixed terminal display faults: most scrambled scrollback in Ghostty on resize, link addresses hidden in Windows Terminal under old tmux and in VTE 0.50.0, and no selection highlight with 16 colors
  • Fixed some garbled rows in tmux with allow-passthrough on inside kitty, Ghostty or iTerm2
  • Fixed /mcp saying no servers were configured after one was added during a session or declined; it now says what to do
  • Fixed /hooks leaving out hooks given by --settings
  • Fixed the / menu listing a row for each skill of the same name, though every row ran the first
  • Fixed /teleport showing no message when the chosen session failed to resume
  • Fixed n and N in transcript search skipping matches
  • Fixed cancelling a transcript search (ctrl+o, then /) in a long session landing far from where the search started
  • Fixed up and down losing the cursor's column over a short or blank line
  • Fixed Tab in shell mode filling in a file name after &&, ; or |, where a command goes
  • Fixed the selected session leaving the screen in claude --resume and /resume when branch names or folder paths are long
  • Fixed the MCP tool list in /mcp and /plugin losing your place when going back from a tool
  • Fixed /resume listing one session fewer than the window has room for, and a 'Resend your message' hint after most spend caps, where resending can't help
  • Fixed an MCP server's long question being cut off after one row, text fields hiding long pastes with no sign, and a doubled divider line in /plugin's options and /login's Bedrock and Vertex steps
  • Fixed the "+N lines" count being too high for command output with links or colors, and the transcript's ? help hiding how to exit in a short window
  • Fixed Ctrl+C twice not closing /chrome from its browser list
  • Fixed a number and Enter typed too early at an agent's plan approval in screen reader mode causing the next number to be dropped too
  • Fixed Claude trying to read design system token files that do not exist when starting a deck or design
  • Fixed exit not saying that a worktree was kept
  • Fixed /hooks help naming input fields that do not exist
  • Fixed question dialogs naming ctrl+g after the external editor key was rebound
  • Fixed two sign-in error messages that pointed to the Claude subscription option on computers where forceLoginMethod is set to console
  • Fixed /config saying the dialog was dismissed instead of "Set theme to …" after changing the theme
  • Bug fixes and reliability improvements
  • Improved the speed of a session's first Bash command: shell start-up files may now run before it's approved, even if it's refused; set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_SHELL_HEAD_START=1 to turn this off
  • Improved commits on newer models and in PowerShell: Claude is now told not to commit files that likely contain secrets
  • Improved sandboxed shell commands: Claude now sees when a command exempt from the sandbox stayed in it because its permission check relied on the sandbox
  • Improved the refusal for shell commands with no rm that the dangerous rm check can't parse, so Claude can resend harmless ones in plain syntax instead of giving up
  • Improved resuming very long sessions: a transcript read that ends early is now retried once, so messages are lost less often
  • Improved subagent answers that hit the output token limit twice: they now more often come back whole or say up front that they are partial
  • Improved long replies on unrecognized models: a reply cut at 32,000 output tokens now continues with a limit of 128,000
  • Improved the reminder about a completed subagent after compaction: if Claude can't read the agent's output file, it is now told to ask the agent with SendMessage
  • Improved the warning shown when an API key and an Anthropic profile are both set: it now says which one is in use and how to switch to the profile
  • Improved /plugin: the question before removing a marketplace now says that its plugins' settings and saved data are deleted, and a marketplace's page no longer shows another marketplace's error
  • Windows: Improved start-up time with no Git Bash and no pwsh on PATH by checking PowerShell's standard install locations at once; System32's powershell.exe now wins over one earlier on PATH
  • Improved startup time on Windows when PATH points to Git for Windows' bin folder, by starting git.exe directly instead of through its launcher
  • Windows: Improved PowerShell tool speed by up to about half a second per command
  • Improved how soon the Bash tool's diff of changed files is ready in auto and bypass permissions modes
  • Improved speed of the Bash permission check on very deeply nested missing paths on macOS and Linux, and of secret masking on very long text with a URL
  • Improved transcript search to find text in edits and written files
  • Improved speed of reading large PNG images, and the quality of the JPEG sent in their place
  • Improved the Artifact tool to read an uploaded file by the address the artifact's page shows; other forms still fail, most with a message that says to read uploads one per call, by id
  • Improved the Artifact tool to ignore prompt, limit and label on some calls that do not use them instead of failing the call
  • Improved MCP server pages in /mcp: local, remote and agent servers share one layout, menus end in Back, and actions are no longer numbered outside screen reader mode; use the arrow keys and Enter
  • Improved narrow terminals: /status, forms and detail screens lay out better, /model and /effort fit at about 40 columns, and key hints such as ←/→ to adjust stay
  • Improved /install-github-app: the repository, secret and API key steps use the standard list and keys, with shorter messages, a spinner and clearer errors
  • Improved /desktop: the download question is a standard list instead of y/n
  • Changed ExitWorktree to ask before removing a worktree that may hold unsaved work; refused in don't-ask mode or with nobody to answer, unless an allow rule, auto or bypass permissions mode allows it
  • Changed claude mcp add --scope project to stop, instead of overwriting the file, when .mcp.json lists its servers at the top level with no mcpServers key
  • Changed the arrow keys on most permission prompts to stop at No instead of wrapping around; a number past the last answer moves to No
  • Changed path checks to refuse some symbolic links
  • Changed what counts as inside a working directory, so some paths now ask for permission
  • Changed permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories to ask about more Bash commands in bypass and auto modes, and to deny some in auto mode
  • Changed permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories to refuse more Bash commands that name a path under a Read or Edit deny rule, where it used to ask
  • Changed auto mode's notice about falling back to billed classifier requests to say that an upcoming release removes the fallback; each action it would have checked will be asked about or denied
  • Changed auto mode to ignore more allow rules that run any package, like Bash(pnpm dlx *), and path or version forms of ones it already ignored (/usr/bin/npm run:*); the safety check decides those
  • Changed /sandbox and most /config value lists to be unnumbered outside screen reader mode; use the arrow keys and Enter
  • Changed Bash commands whose variables expand to very long text to be denied, with a message that says to use shorter values or a file
  • Changed the PowerShell tool to ask before one more command, even under a rule naming it; if nothing answers, it's refused unless a whole-tool rule, auto mode or bypass permissions mode allows it
  • Changed a subagent resumed by a sibling's message to follow the session's permission settings; it may now ask, or be refused where nobody can answer
  • Changed --worktree with a relative --add-dir beside the launch folder to give the Bash sandbox that folder, not one beside the worktree
  • Changed some --worktree starts with a relative --add-dir above the launch folder, such as .., to give the Bash sandbox, and a --bg session, only the worktree
  • Changed Claude in Chrome to refuse uploading some credential files; attach those to the page yourself
  • Changed artifact approval in organizations that require it for each new artifact: an artifact that only a plugin created or allowed can be refused
  • Changed sessions with nobody to ask to refuse a new artifact at once, with no permission prompt, in organizations that require approval of each one
  • Changed the Artifact tool to refuse calls once settings turn Artifacts off, in sessions already running too
  • Changed the Artifact publish prompt to stop offering "don't ask again" in subagents and after a background task result, someone else's message or a compaction
  • Changed claude plugin eval to keep its deny rules over a plugin's permission hook, and to flag calls the hook let through
  • Changed MCP server logs to record the mode, action, and field names of elicitation requests and hook answers, not their full contents
  • Changed most prompts to ignore answers other than Esc for a moment after resuming with fg
  • Changed Code Mode to no longer refuse to start when an installed mod hooks tool calls; an administrator can still keep Code Mode off in managed settings
  • Changed subagents launched without a model to stay on the model they started on when resumed, including after /model
  • Changed the first subagent on a model to wait up to 1.5 seconds (10 in claude -p) for that model's settings from Anthropic, instead of starting without them
  • Changed restarted background subagents, and turns that start by themselves, to wait for plugins to load
  • Changed prompt history to leave out most launch prompts of sessions that another Claude Code session started, such as claude --bg run by Claude
  • Changed subagent progress summaries in terminal sessions on Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI and Microsoft Foundry to be written from short notes, not the whole conversation, using far fewer tokens
  • Changed non-interactive (-p) mode to run fewer git commands before the first request
  • Changed first-run setup to skip terminal setup in remote VS Code, Cursor and Devin Desktop sessions, where it cannot change settings
  • Changed fullscreen text selection to leave out the glyph of system, thinking and inbound message lines
  • Changed Anthropic-hosted cloud sessions to ignore more of a repository's flag and plugin delivery settings; its CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC now acts at most as DISABLE_TELEMETRY
  • [VSCode] Added "Claude Code: Add to Chat" to the Explorer's right-click menu, which @-mentions the selected files and folders in the chat
  • [VSCode] Fixed the permission prompt not showing the reason that a PreToolUse hook gives when it asks for confirmation (#85950)
  • [VSCode] Fixed long tool and file names being cut off in a permission prompt's title
  • [VSCode] Fixed a terminal session's diff showing the previous proposed edit after you typed in it and Claude edited the same file again
  • [VSCode] Fixed Escape also stopping Claude's response when it closes the feedback or "Build a custom style" dialog, the @-mention menu, the model, mode or "+" menu, or another popup
  • [VSCode] Improved speed when Claude makes several edits in a row: queued edits share one wait for new problems; a problem may be reported with a later edit
  • [VSCode] Improved @-mention file search speed in large workspaces when rg is on your PATH; results now rank much as in the terminal, with less tolerance for typos
  • [VSCode] Improved startup: the model picker is ready at once in folders opened for the first time, empty windows and worktrees, except on third-party providers
  • [VSCode] Changed a chat edit's diff to stay open and keep asking for approval when a terminal session in the same window sends a prompt
  • [VSCode] Removed unused tools from the IDE connection (openFile, saveDocument, getOpenEditors and related)

items.summary:
Triton Inference Server

The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application.

New Features and Improvements

  • PyTorch backend: Added AOTI BF16 input/output support.
  • THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt is now included in the containers.
  • Fixed a use-after-free in the dynamic batcher and a preserve_ordering completion-slot issue on response-cache hits.
  • Prevented silent gRPC stream cancellations under backpressure.
  • Bounded the decompressed HTTP inference response size in the client library.
  • Perf Analyzer: Honored supplied output shapes, propagated the binary exit code, tagged the wheel as platform-specific, and limited profile-data export to the needed inputs and outputs.
  • Python backend: Now logs when the backend stub exits on a crash signal.

Known Issues

  • The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.
  • vLLM's v0 API and Ray are affected by vulnerabilities. Users should consider their own architecture and mitigation steps which may include but should not be limited to:
    • Do not expose Ray executors and vLLM hosts to a network where any untrusted connections might reach the host.
    • Ensure that only the other vLLM hosts are able to connect to the TCP port used for the XPUB socket. Note that the port used is random.
  • When using Valgrind or other leak detection tools on AGX-Thor or DGX-Spark systems, you might see memory leaks attributed to NvRmGpuLibOpen.
  • Valgrind or other memory leak detection tools may occasionally report leaks related to DCGM. These reports are intermittent and often disappear on retry.
  • CuPy has issues with the CUDA 13 Device API in multithreaded contexts. Avoid using tritonclient cuda_shared_memory APIs in multithreaded environments until fixed by CuPy.
  • TensorRT calibration cache may require size adjustment in some cases, which was observed for the IGX platform.
  • The core Python binding may incur an additional D2H and H2D copy if the backend and frontend both specify device memory to be used for response tensors.
  • A segmentation fault related to DCGM and NSCQ may be encountered during server shutdown on NVSwitch systems. A possible workaround for this issue is to disable the collection of GPU metrics tritonserver --allow-gpu-metrics false ....
  • When using TensorRT models, if auto-complete configuration is disabled and is_non_linear_format_io:true for reformat-free tensors is not provided in the model configuration, the model may not load successfully.
  • When using Python models in decoupled mode, users need to ensure that the ResponseSender goes out of scope or is properly cleaned up before unloading the model to guarantee that the unloading process executes correctly.
  • Triton Inference Server with vLLM backend currently does not support running vLLM models with tensor parallelism sizes greater than 1 and the default "distributed_executor_backend" setting when using explicit model control mode. In attempt to load a vllm model (tp > 1) in explicit mode, users could potentially see failure at initialize step: could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads. For the default model control mode, after server shutdown, vllm related sub-processes are not killed. Related vllm issue: vllm-project/vllm#6766. Please specify "distributed_executor_backend":"ray" in the model.json when deploying vllm models with tensor parallelism > 1.
  • When loading models with file override, multiple model configuration files are not supported. Users must provide the model configuration by setting parameter "config" : "<JSON>" instead of custom configuration file in the following format: "file:configs/<model-config-name>.pbtxt" : "<base64-encoded-file-content>".
  • TensorRT-LLM backend provides limited support of Triton extensions and features.
  • The TensorRT-LLM backend may core dump on server shutdown. This impacts server teardown only and will not impact inferencing.
  • The Java CAPI is known to have intermittent segfaults.
  • Some systems which implement malloc() may not release memory back to the operating system right away causing a false memory leak. This can be mitigated by using a different malloc implementation. Tcmalloc and jemalloc are installed in the Triton container and can be used by specifying the library in LD_PRELOAD. NVIDIA recommends experimenting with both tcmalloc and jemalloc to determine which one works better for your use case.
  • Auto-complete may cause an increase in server start time. To avoid a start time increase, users can provide the full model configuration and launch the server with --disable-auto-complete-config.
  • Auto-complete does not support PyTorch models due to lack of metadata in the model. It can only verify that the number of inputs and the input names matches what is specified in the model configuration. There is no model metadata about the number of outputs and datatypes. Related PyTorch bug: pytorch/pytorch#38273
  • Triton Client PIP wheels for ARM SBSA are not available from PyPI and pip will install an incorrect Jetson version of Triton Client library for Arm SBSA. The correct client wheel file can be pulled directly from the Arm SBSA SDK image and manually installed.
  • Traced models in PyTorch seem to create overflows when int8 tensor values are transformed to int32 on the GPU. Refer to pytorch/pytorch#66930 for more information.
  • Triton cannot retrieve GPU metrics with MIG-enabled GPU devices.
  • Triton metrics might not work if the host machine is running a separate DCGM agent on bare-metal or in a container.

Client Libraries and Examples

The client libraries and examples are available in this release exclusively via the Ubuntu 24.04–based NGC Container. The SDK container includes the client libraries and examples, Performance Analyzer, and Model Analyzer. See Getting the Client Libraries for more information.

ManyLinux Assets (early access)

This release was compiled with AlmaLinux 8.9 based out of manylinux_2_34 and can be used on RHEL 9 and later versions.
See the included README.md for complete details about installation, verification, and support.
This release supports ensembles. Confirm CUDA, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, and Python versions in the shipped README.md.
Some optional backend features such as the PyTorch backend's TorchTRT extension are not currently supported.
